 Vilma Rios Thu, October 22, 2026 at 3:00 PM MST 6 min read Quick Read 
 Retirees who skip withholding on IRA and Social Security income can owe nearly $4,931 in federal taxes by April with no payments made during the year. 
 A December IRA withdrawal with tax withheld spreads the payment equally across all four quarters, retroactively eliminating penalties for missed deadlines. 
 Joint filers with provisional income above $44,000 owe taxes on up to 85% of Social Security benefits, a rule many new retirees don't discover until April. 
 Read More: Avoid these 13 retirement mistakes before they derail your future (sponsor) 
 For decades, an employer covered the hardest part of your tax bill: paying it. Every paycheck sent a portion to the IRS. Then the paychecks stop, IRA withdrawals and Social Security deposits take over, and in many households nobody sends the IRS anything until April. 
 John Keith / Shutterstock.com That gap costs money. Federal law requires you to pay tax as the income comes in. Retirees who wait until filing season can owe the full bill plus an underpayment penalty under Section 6654 of the Internal Revenue Code. Here's how the trap forms, and the year-end fix that can still rescue 2026. 
 How a Quiet First Year of Retirement Turns Into a $4,900 April Bill 
 Consider a sample couple, age 67, in their first full year without wages in 2026. They collect the average Social Security benefit for an aged couple, $3,208 a month, and pull $60,000 from a traditional IRA. To keep every dollar, they told the custodian to withhold nothing. 
 Here's their 2026 federal math on a joint return:

 Amount

 $3,300

 Tax paid during the year

 Their taxable income fits the 10% bracket, which runs to $24,800 on a joint return in 2026. Only the dollars above that line are taxed at 12%.

 Section 6654 Wants Your Tax in Four Installments 
 Section 6654 splits each year's tax into 4 required installments, due April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15 of the following year. Miss them and the IRS charges a penalty that works like interest, figured separately for each late quarter. 
 There are two escape exits. You owe no penalty if the tax due after withholding comes to less than $1,000. You're also safe if you paid the smaller of 90% of this year's tax or 100% of last year's. That second figure rises to 110% if last year's adjusted gross income exceeded $150,000. 
 Our couple misses both. To hit the 90% line, they needed to pay about $4,438 for 2026, or roughly $1,109 per quarter. Three of those deadlines have already passed. 
 Social Security Taxes Supercharge the Bill 
 Plenty of new retirees assume Social Security is tax-free. Under Section 86, joint filers whose provisional income (other income plus half of benefits) passes $44,000 can owe tax on up to 85% of their benefits. Our couple's provisional income reached $79,248, so the full 85% counts as taxable. 
 The new senior deduction softens the hit. It's worth $6,000 per person 65 or older for tax years starting before January 1, 2029. It shrinks by 6% of modified AGI above $150,000 on a joint return. Bank interest adds to the total, too. A 12-month CD yield averaged 1.76% nationally on October 1, 2026, the highest reading in a year, and every dollar of that interest is taxable. 
 A December IRA Withdrawal Can Fix Missed Quarterly Payments 
 Under Section 6654(g)(1), tax withheld during the year counts as paid in equal parts on each due date, no matter when it actually came out of your account. Estimated payments don't get that treatment. A check mailed in December covers the fourth quarter alone. 
 That means our couple can take an IRA distribution in December 2026 and have at least $4,438 withheld for federal tax. The IRS spreads that money evenly across all four quarters, which can eliminate the penalty on the three deadlines they already missed. 
 Two other options help from here on: 
 Keep the IRA default. Custodians must withhold 10% of one-time distributions unless you opt out on Form W-4R. On their withdrawals, that comes to $6,000, more than the couple's entire bill. 
 Withhold from Social Security. File Form W-4V, or ask online, to withhold 7%, 10%, 12%, or 22% of each monthly payment. 
 If you'd rather pay the IRS directly, the fourth 2026 installment is due January 15, 2027. 
 Costliest Mistake: Choosing Zero Withholding to Keep More Cash 
 Opting out of the 10% default feels like keeping your money. All it really does is push the bill to April and add a penalty on top. Rerun the numbers every year, because Social Security's 3.6% cost-of-living raise for 2027 pushes provisional income up on its own. 
 State income taxes vary widely, and some states exempt Social Security or pension income, so your state bill may look very different from your federal one. Setting withholding across IRA withdrawals, Social Security and any Roth conversions is math worth running with a CPA before December 31 (the underpayment penalty is just one of nine IRS rules that quietly drain retirement accounts, all charted in our free tax trap map).
